evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 甲骨文 and 金文 usage
evidence.text: The database describes 人 in ancient forms as a person standing in profile with hands lowered; it gives the original sense as ‘person’. It cites Shang oracle-bone examples 《合集》22626 ‘伐十人’ (ten people killed) and 《合集》20328 ‘余一人’ (the king’s self-reference), and bronze-inscription uses including ‘庶人’ (common people) and ‘人民’. It also reports a bronze-inscription phonetic loan 人 for 年 in one vessel inscription, a separate graph borrowing from 人’s role as sound element in 年.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析: 人

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry identifies the graph in oracle-bone inscriptions (合集6175), bronze inscriptions (集成00944), and the Small Seal script / Shuowen. Its account interprets the profile figure’s upper end as the head, middle as body, one extended stroke as arm, and lower part as legs. This supports a human-figure pictograph analysis; the stroke-by-stroke description is the database’s interpretation, not a separately demonstrated chronology.
evidence.title: 漢字「人」：字形演變

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The page labels the early forms as oracle-bone, bronze, Chu-script bamboo/silk, and Small Seal / Shuowen, and identifies the character as U+4EBA. These corpus labels establish the kinds of forms represented, but the page does not date an individual oracle-bone specimen or provide a semantic chronology.
evidence.title: 漢字「人」：字形演變

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 研訂瀏覽; historical form claims
evidence.text: The entry quotes Shuowen’s account that 人 depicts arm and shin forms, then cautions that certain ‘ancient’ shapes reported in later reference works are not found in oracle-bone, bronze, or ancient Zhou-script materials and their evidence is unknown. This warns against treating all forms labelled ancient as genuine early ancestors. It does not dispute the ordinary profile-person analysis supported by the paleographic databases.
evidence.title: 教育部《異體字字典》 [A00068] 人

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry records the modern Mandarin pronunciation rén. It also discusses later written variants, including a form said in historical dictionaries to have been created under Wu Zetian. These are variant-history observations, not evidence for the graph’s original formation or a sound-component role.
evidence.title: 教育部《異體字字典》 [A00068] 人

evidence.field: Unihan database scope and reading-field status
evidence.text: Unicode describes Unihan as a repository of character data that includes readings; its documentation says readings vary across periods and places and should not be treated as evidence for ancient sound relations. The supplied local row is kMandarin 人 = rén in sources/unihan/Unihan_Readings.txt (exact row was provided in the input); the matching supplied Baxter–Sagart row is 人, Mandarin ren, MC nyin, OC *ni[ŋ] in sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv. These local rows are recorded as dataset readings, not as proof of etymology. The requested character-specific Unicode Unihan page was inaccessible, so neither local row is externally verified through that click-through page.
evidence.title: Unicode Standard Annex #38: Unicode Han Database (Unihan)

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry separately reports oracle-bone 人 borrowed for the state-name graph 夷 in the phrase 人方, and bronze 人 borrowed for 年 in one inscription. These are claims about whole-graph loans in particular attestations. They should not be confused with the role of 人 as a phonetic element within another graph, and the page does not give enough phonological detail to establish either borrowing’s sound correspondence independently here.

search_audit.outcome: Inspected the CUHK character entry, which supplies Shang-period examples, graph borrowing claims, and later bronze-script extensions. Other results were not used because they were secondary, general, or not directly relevant.

gaps: The oldest forms are labelled oracle-bone and bronze forms in the paleographic database, but the inspected page does not date the individual cited specimens; the oracle-bone corpus context is broadly Late Shang, not a character-specific first-use date.
No independent external verification of the supplied Baxter–Sagart table row was possible, and no same-system comparison is needed for 人 itself because it has no proposed sound component.

The official character-specific Unihan endpoint https://www.unicode.org/cgi-bin/GetUnihanData.pl?codepoint=4EBA was attempted but inaccessible in the web tool. The local exact kMandarin row was supplied and retained as local metadata only; it is not represented as externally verified.

Shuowen’s account is an early historical explanation, not independent confirmation of a pristine pictorial origin. Inspected modern paleographic references support the side-profile human interpretation, but no glyph image was visually inspected in this research.

The source database offers selected older semantic uses, but not a systematic chronology of all extensions such as individual, people, someone, or other person. No chronology is inferred from modern gloss lists.

The reported 人-for-夷 and 人-for-年 loans are source assertions. Their precise early pronunciations and the phonological basis of each loan were not independently established in this search. No claim is made that 人 derives from 仁 or vice versa.
